About

An engineer by education. A designer by curiosity.

I’ve always wanted to know how things work. These days that means people, products, and the wonderfully complicated systems in between.

Chapter 01 · The engineer

It started with how machines work.

I studied Mechanical Engineering, then a master’s in Design Engineering, where I led and published my own research work. I learned to take a problem apart before putting anything back together.

Chapter 02 · The designer

Same curiosity. A different kind of machine.

Design turned out to be engineering, but with people in the loop. And people are why I stayed.

I watch people closely, closely enough to do impressions of most of them. Design is the same game played seriously: predicting what someone will do in a moment, and you get better not just by guessing well, but by understanding them, and the world around them, a little more each day. It takes a head for systems and a heart for people.

The problem

Two weeks into the quarter, Angela, a contract manager, gets one question from her finance lead: which high-value contracts renew this quarter, and which should we renegotiate? Renewals are where contract value is protected. Miss a notice window and an agreement can roll into another term on old rates; catch it in time and it becomes the moment to renegotiate pricing, tighten terms or exit a supplier that no longer fits.

The answer exists, but it is spread across the repository. Angela filters a search, rebuilds the numbers in a BI report, checks a saved view, exports to Excel, then opens contracts and amendments one by one to confirm the dates. By the time her list is ready, some of those windows are already closing.

What if Angela could simply ask?

For users, search is not the goal; the decision is. They need to find the right information fast, understand it in context, and act with confidence before a deadline.

My role

My role was to turn a chat box into a way to reach a decision.

I believe AI should fit into the places, objects and habits people already have, not replace them. So I designed how AskSirion understands a question, shapes its answer, and lives inside Sirion’s existing structure.

Step 1 of 3 · From questions to intent

I read 201 questions as 201 decisions.

Legal and the PM had collected the questions real users ask. I treated that golden dataset as research, not a test set.

  1. I framed the ideal answer to each question, with the PM: what someone needs to see to act, not just what the database returns.
  2. I looked behind each question for the intent. “Which contracts renew this quarter?” is really “what do I need to act on before the notice dates?”
  3. I grouped the questions by intent into seven answer types, so each type was designed once, not question by question.
ListingAcross the portfolio, by field type
One contractAsked by its ID

Why it mattered The model now had a target: not just “answer correctly”, but “answer the way this person decides”.

Step 2 of 3 · Shape the answer

I shaped each answer around where its information lives.

Left alone, the model wrote long, hedged paragraphs. I designed the expected answer for each type, refined it with the PM, and let the source of the information decide its shape.

Three answer types, one per level · pick one to see it

The more spread out the information, the more structure the answer needs. The more precise it is, the more proof it shows.

    Step 3 of 3 · Connect the architecture

    The AI works through the product, not around it.

    Contract information in Sirion lives at three levels: portfolio, contract and document. Instead of a separate AI space, every answer lands on the level it belongs to and opens in the native Sirion view.

    I definedthe levels, how questions land on them, the answer form at eachThe wider systemthe data hierarchy and level detection

    My call The AI complements the existing architecture. It never routes the user around it.

    A consequence

    One consequence: the subject can change silently.

    Moving by asking“Show me CO04107” narrows the conversation from the whole portfolio to one contract, inside the chat.
    Moving by clickingFiltering a chart, clicking a count or opening a contract changes the scope just as much, outside the chat.
    The riskThe next question, “which of these renew?”, now refers to something the user may not realise has changed. The wrong scope gives a confident, wrong answer.

    Once people could move by asking and by clicking, the scope could shift without anyone saying so. A permanent indicator names the current scope, explains it, and resets in one click.

    States from the shipped context indicator.

    I definedthe indicator, its states and copy, the reset, the rule that earlier answers stay fixed

    My call Context is never silent. If the subject changes, the interface says so before the user asks the next question.

    Impact AskSirion works inside Sirion, not beside it: answers open in the native views, and the context indicator is in production.

    Where it got hard

    The model could answer. Making that answer usable meant solving problems the model didn’t solve for us.

    They came from the people using it, from language itself, and from the shape of a conversation. Each became its own piece of work.

    What changed because of it

    Shipped April 2024. Still the foundation of Sirion’s conversational layer.

    In the product todayThe four-part answer anatomy (sources, answer, evidence, related), unchanged since April 2024. The restate-then-count response pattern. The interpretation chips, the four-part reasoning and the Refine panel. The context indicator with reset. The disambiguation framework and its confidence thresholds. Fork. And the Prompt Library of 2026, which solved the blank-canvas problem I first tried to solve with suggestion cards in 2023, at far greater depth.
    In how the team workedThe response sheet, around thirty scenarios in seven categories with six failure states, became the contract between design and engineering: a shape to fill and something to test against. The edge-case matrix I wrote before launch meant engineering never had to guess what the answer should do in a corner case. The golden dataset became research, not just a test set.
    In where the product wentAfter launch, power users came to a dedicated AskSirion screen; most contract managers stayed in the listings they knew. I moved AskSirion into the listing, contract and document views instead, carrying their context with them. A companion, not a destination. The concept screen I drew in late 2023 asked AskSirion to amend contracts, an instruction rather than a question, before anyone in the industry said “agentic”. The scope model, context and evidence route from this work are the ground the agents now stand on.

    Described publicly on Sirion’s product page, in the September 2025 release notes and at the October 2025 launch.

    What I know now

    AI earns trust by fitting in, not by taking over.

    Trust comes from being understandable.Every feature I’m proudest of exists because people could see the reading, the steps and the source, not because the model was right more often.
    Systems outlast screens.The answer anatomy, the response pattern, the edge-case matrix and the disambiguation framework outlived every visual refinement around them.
    Meet people where they already work.They didn’t change their workflow for the AI; I changed the AI for their workflow.
    What I’d do differently

    Instrument from day one, so the claims above come with numbers. Sit in customer calls myself instead of inheriting the pain points. And treat the blank canvas as a design problem from the start, not two and a half years in.

    The problem

    In AskSirion, an answer is never just an answer. It’s structured to help someone decide, and it’s full of doors: every count, chart, row and contract opens onto something deeper. Angela asks for Northwind contracts with a COLA clause and gets 116. Before she asks anything else, she walks through a few of those doors: she opens the list, narrows it to EMEA from the chart, and opens a contract that looks off. Then she types “which of these renew this year?” Every door had moved her somewhere new, but the system only followed her words. What “these” meant depended on rules nobody could see.

    Asking · 1 way
    Ask a new question
    The next question is about116 contracts
    Clicking · 6 ways
    Click a count in an old answer
    Filter the list
    Click a chart
    Open a contract
    Open a document
    Go back up the thread

    Seven doors out of one answer. Six of them aren’t questions.

    From my research board: every action that changes context, marked on the real screens. This is where the seven doors came from.

    Where this sits

    This isn’t only AskSirion’s problem.

    Research on conversational analytics found follow-up questions behaving unexpectedly once people interact with a chart. AI coding tools pass along the file you’re in, and show it above the input. But none of them had to follow someone through three levels of contract data, into datasets no answer contained. There was no pattern to borrow, so I defined one.

    Kind of toolWhere context comes fromWhat they didn’t have to face
    General chat assistants
    The conversation, plus what you attachA structured space to move through between questions
    AI coding assistants
    The file or selection you’re in, often shown as chips above the inputMore than one level, datasets built by hand, going back into old answers
    Visual analytics research
    References to a chart and to earlier sentencesA multi-level repository instead of a single chart
    AskSirion
    Every door: counts in old answers, filters, charts, contracts, documentsThree levels, hand-built datasets no answer contained, and data that changes over time

    Sources: Tableau Research, Evizeon (VAST 2017); GitHub Copilot context passing and community discussion; the Cursor forum.

    People will always explore. AskSirion should follow them through every door, register exactly where they are, and answer the next question from there.

    My role

    My role was to make AskSirion follow people wherever they explore, then show them where it thinks they are.

    I learned how the system tracked context from the developers, then defined a new model myself, along with the interface that communicates it. I validated both with the PM when I presented the solution.

    Step 1 of 3 · Teach it to follow

    I defined what the system has to listen to.

    Every click is a move. I wrote down what context is made of and how each move updates it, so engineering could build a system that follows, and design could explain it.

    Context slides forwardEach answer builds on the last two steps, so the thread stays coherent without carrying everything.

    Clicks never answerOpening a contract or a document changes the scope, but never fires a response by itself.
    Learned from engineeringhow the system tracked context beforeI definedthe precedence model, the sliding window and its rulesValidated with the PMwhen I presented the solution

    My call Clicks change the scope. Only questions produce answers.

    Impact Engineering had one rule set to build against, and design had one model to explain.

    Step 2 of 3 · Show where it’s following

    I put the scope where the decision is made.

    Following silently isn’t enough: people need to see where the system thinks they are. My first assumption was that the interface already showed it. A scrolled chat proved it didn’t. So I designed one permanent indicator above the composer: four kinds of scope, an explanation on demand, and a one-click reset.

    Step 3 of 3 · Keep the answer true to its moment

    A question remembers what it was asked about.

    A question asked from a hand-built dataset is answered at the bottom of the thread, never inserted into the past. A chip above it names that dataset, and clicking it reopens the exact list in the content panel.

    Today

    3

    Nothing above changes. Out-of-turn questions land at the bottom, and earlier answers keep their original counts.

    I definedthe chip and what it reopens, answer placement, the scope line in answers

    My call The thread never rewrites itself. Earlier answers keep the counts they were given.

    Impact A dataset people built by hand, which no answer contained, became something they could return to.

    Where it got hard

    Following is easy when people move forward. These were the moments they didn’t.

    A scrolled chatScroll up and the visible answer no longer matches the active scope. The indicator stays put, whatever is on screen.
    Yesterday’s numbersAn old answer’s count may no longer be true today. Earlier answers keep their original counts, and the chip reopens what was actually asked about.
    ResettingWhen the scope is cleared, where does the conversation continue? At the bottom, from the latest question, never from a guess.
    What changed because of it

    All of it shipped.

    In the productThe indicator with four scope types, explanation and reset; out-of-turn answers at the bottom that restate their scope; the chip that reopens its dataset.
    In how the team workedOne precedence model that engineering builds against and design explains, instead of behaviour discovered case by case.
    PubliclySirion’s September 2025 release notes describe the scope indicator in production.

    Next I’d measure how often people reset the scope, open a chip, or rephrase a question because the scope was wrong.

    What I know now

    Follow first, then show.

    Define behaviour before interfaceThe indicator was only possible because the model underneath it was written down first.
    Show it at the moment of decisionStatus shown anywhere else is status nobody reads.
    Restraint is a featureThree plausible signals were cut so one could be trusted.
    What I’d do differently

    Test the edge cases with real people earlier: the scrolled-chat problem showed up on a whiteboard, not in a session. And instrument resets and chip opens from day one.

    Alternate Interpretations
    Explanation

    In contract data, terms like ‘value’ and ‘initiated’ can point to a few different fields.

    • ‘Value’ relates with

    The problem

    People talk like humans. The system thinks like a database.

    Search has wrestled with ambiguity for as long as search boxes have existed. What changed is that the system now guesses, with a confidence score, instead of following rules. A sentence can mean more than one thing at the same time. A database query can’t. Once AskSirion let people ask in their own words, every question had to be turned into exactly one set of fields and values, and the system was forced to pick one meaning and run with it, even when several were equally valid. That is where the confusion started.

    “Show me high value contracts above 10 million”
    Total Contract Valueoverall valueWhat the system picked
    Committed Contract Valuevalue under TD programsWhat she meant
    Maximum Contract Valuethe ceiling a contract allows
    Estimated Annual Spenda yearly estimate
    She gets the wrong contracts.She stops trusting the answer.The AI feels like it’s “acting smart but giving nonsense”.

    Every reading is correct. Only one is what she meant.

    Help people land on the right reading quickly, without having to reword the question.

    Where ambiguity comes from

    It comes from the schema, not the user.

    I went through the questions people asked and sorted every ambiguity by its cause. Almost none were sloppy questions. They were reasonable phrases that the contract schema holds in more than one place. Four kinds covered nearly all of them.

    Date × Date
    “contracts starting in 2024”
    Effective dateSignature date
    Number × Number
    “high value contracts”
    Total contract valueCommitted value
    Logic
    “fees allowed and notification required”
    Both must hold (AND)Either can hold (OR)
    Entity
    “contracts for Northwind”
    As counterpartyAs domestic clientAs global client

    My call Treat ambiguity as a property of the data, not a mistake by the user. The fix belongs to the system.

    The first plan

    Prevent it, interpret it, recover from it.

    My first framework had three stages. Prevent ambiguity while the question is being typed, with field-aware autocomplete and chips. Interpret it after submission, by generating every valid reading and ranking them. Recover after the results, with a way to switch readings in one click.

    Stage 1 · While typingPrevent

    Autocomplete, smart chips and field suggestions stop ambiguity before the question runs.

    Cut: not feasible
    Stage 2 · After submittingInterpret

    Generate the valid readings, rank them, run the strongest, keep the others ready.

    Stage 3 · After the resultsRecover

    Show the other readings beside the answer and switch in one click.

    The real blocker

    Typing moves in milliseconds. Understanding took seconds.

    While someone types “S… h… o… w… c… o…”, the system would have to:

    Read a half-written sentenceUnderstand its meaningMatch it to the whole contract databasePredict the intentSuggest the right field
    in under 200 milliseconds
    A keystroke100–200 ms
    Interpreting a question~10 s

    Not happening.

    Engineering was clear that typing-time intelligence wasn’t technically feasible. So I cut the stage instead of shipping a weak version of it: an autocomplete that guesses wrongly while you type is worse than none. Interpretation and recovery had to carry the whole problem.

    My call Design the stages the system can actually deliver. Two strong stages beat three where one is pretend.

    The core decision

    Ask first, or answer first?

    Every AI search has to choose. Asking first is safe and slow. Answering first is fast and sometimes wrong, and it hides a quieter failure I call the Netflix-profile trap: a system that keeps inferring what you meant instead of simply asking. I designed both, side by side, on the same question, to see what each one costs.

    Exploration sketches. The two directions were compared side by side before any visual design.

    Neither was right on its own. Asking every time punishes the people who asked clearly; answering every time punishes the people the system misread.

    Research and validation

    Before committing to either, I went looking for who had solved this before.

    Ambiguity isn’t new, so I treated the choice as a research question. I went back to Greg Nudelman’s 2009 column on query disambiguation, read what current research says about language models (they rarely ask for clarification and tend to commit to a single reading), and wrote to Greg himself about how this changes when the AI interprets intent. The Digital Twin exercise from his book UX for AI gave me a way to decide what the model should and shouldn’t guess.

    What carried over from 2009
    E-commerce search, 2009AskSirion, 2025
    Select a default category

    Chosen from what the inventory holds and what people picked before, once it passes a threshold.

    →
    Run the strongest reading

    Chosen by a score built from field importance and user and organisation history, against confidence thresholds.

    Show related searches

    The most common ways people refined the same query.

    →
    Offer alternate interpretations

    Each one a full question that can be re-run in one click.

    Display a category selector

    Let people choose the meaning themselves.

    →
    Ask a clarifying question

    Only when confidence is genuinely low, with two or three options.

    One of his findings stayed with me. A vague undo link, “Not looking for Nike Shoes?”, went unnoticed in testing, while links that named the other categories were the ones that worked. It is the same reason every alternate in AskSirion names its field instead of asking “Did you mean…?”.

    Answer by defaultA default reading is what search has always done well. The risk is doing it silently, so the answer has to say which reading ran.
    Ask only when it mattersResearch and practice agree that when to ask is the hard part. That needed a measure, not a rule of thumb.
    Name the alternativeA vague “Did you mean…?” goes unnoticed. Every other reading has to say exactly what it changes.

    My call Answer first, ask only when confidence is low, and make every alternative name its field. The next question was how to measure confidence.

    The framework

    First, a score for every reading.

    Research said when to ask was the hard part. To decide it, we had to agree on how sure the system actually is. An enterprise can have hundreds of contract fields, and one word in a question can point at several of them, so tuning them by hand was never an option. I worked with the PM and engineering on a formula that scores any reading, for any organisation, using what the product already knows.

    For each reading final_score =(parser_confidence)− (competing_readings × penalty)+ (field_importance_weight)+ (user/org_history_weight)+ (semantic_similarity_weight)

    Designing the responses

    Two responses, designed in detail: one that answers and offers, one that stops and asks.

    The framework decided which response a question gets. Most of my design work went into the two that carry the ambiguity: answering while offering the other readings, and asking without blocking the conversation.

    1 · Answer, and offer the other readings

    Every part of the answer had to earn its place.

    It started as a single “Did you mean this?” chip under the answer. That proved the idea, but it offered one alternative and gave no reason. So I rebuilt the response part by part, and wrote down what each part was for.

    I found 100 Contracts where the Total Contract Value exceeds $10 million.

    In contract data, terms like ‘value’ and ‘initiated’ can point to a few different fields. ‘Value’ might be total, committed or maximum value…

    Here are other ways your question could be interpreted. I will refresh the results based on your choice.

    1The answer comes first

    People always get an immediate answer, even when the question was imperfect. AskSirion stays responsive, not demanding.

    2Then why it was ambiguous

    It reassures people that ambiguity is normal, not an error, gives them a mental model of how the fields differ, and opens the door to asking more precisely next time.

    3Then the other readings, as whole questions

    No mechanical picking of field chips. Each option is a complete thought, so people don’t assemble meaning from pieces: they simply pick the version they meant.

    The placement dilemma

    Where should the explanation live?

    The explanation was the part that made the alternates make sense, and the part most likely to clutter every answer. I tried it in three places before settling on a fourth.

    Between the answer and the alternates

    I found 100 Contracts…

    In contract data, terms like ‘value’ and ‘initiated’ can point to a few different fields. ‘Value’ might be total, committed or maximum value…

    Always seen, but every ambiguous answer grows longer and the choices get pushed down.

    At the end, behind “More”
    Interpretation summary
    More ›

    The answer stays short, but the reason sits after the choices it explains, and few people open it.

    Inside the reasoning
    3 Steps ⌃
    ✓ Value identification‘Value’ mapped to Total Contract Value…
    ✓ Field search and expansionAlso matches committed and maximum value…

    It fits how the system explains itself, but the reasoning is about its own steps, not the user’s words, and it is collapsed by default.

    Behind an Explain tag ✓
    Alternate InterpretationsExplain
    Explanation‘Value’ relates with
    Total Contract ValueCommitted ValueMaximum Value

    Right beside the alternates it explains, there when wanted. And it stopped being a paragraph: a card that names the words and the fields, with the one used highlighted.

    My call Explain on demand, right next to the choice it explains, and show it as structure, not prose.

    The subtle part

    Choosing the other reading doesn’t mean the system was wrong.

    Both readings were logically correct, just mutually exclusive. Picking the alternate only means the user chose a valid reading the system couldn’t confidently rank first. That changed what a switch should do. If the new result simply replaced the old one, the user would lose trust, control and traceability, which matter more in contract work than almost anywhere else.

    Keep the originalThe first answer, on the first reading, stays where it was.
    Generate the alternateThe other reading runs as its own answer, with its own count and columns.
    Switch back freelyMoving between the two is one click, in either direction.
    Option 1 · Versions in place
    Show me high value contracts…
    ‹ 2/2 ›

    The answer keeps both readings as versions you can step between, like editing a prompt in ChatGPT.

    Option 2 · A fork
    Generating your answer in a new chat

    The alternate opens as a new conversation, the same way Fork works elsewhere in AskSirion, and the original thread is untouched.

    My call A switch should add an answer, never erase one. In contract work, the trail matters as much as the result.

    2 · Stop and ask, without blocking

    A question that takes the composer’s place, not the conversation’s.

    When confidence is low, the system asks. I designed the question as a card that sits where the composer usually is, so people answer where they would have typed, and nothing on screen is locked behind a modal. Once it’s answered, it folds away; if it’s set aside, it waits.

    The rules I wrote down

    Seven guidelines, so every ambiguous answer behaves the same way.

    Clarity over concealmentAlways show what the system understood. Never hide the reading.
    One-click correctionSwitching to another reading is a single click, never a rewrite.
    Don’t block the answerThe primary result appears immediately, unless confidence is genuinely low.
    Don’t shame the userAlternates are the system’s readings, not the user’s mistakes.
    Show what changedHighlight the exact field or logic that differs between readings.
    Group similar readingsOrganise alternates by kind: dates together, values together.
    Four at mostNever show more than four alternates. Pick the likeliest.
    I definedthe framework, the four types, the confidence bands and their behaviours, the recovery UI, the switching model, the guidelinesCo-designed with product & engineeringthe confidence formula and its thresholds, worked out with the PM and engineeringThe wider systemthe parser and the ranking model
    What changed because of it

    The system stopped pretending to be sure.

    In the productMost of the framework shipped. Answers carry their alternate readings with a one-click switch and an Explain, and low-confidence questions get a short choice instead of a guess. The same idea runs through AskSirion’s progressive clarifications, like asking which manager field someone means.
    What came nextThe learning score grew into Memory V1, which I took from discovery to launch: it keeps clarifications, field mappings and terminology at the user level, and is delete-only so nothing it remembers is silently rewritten.
    Where the field landedThe same split I designed now shows up in research and guidelines: decide when to ask, what to ask, and how to respond after, and disambiguate before acting when in doubt.

    No measured result is claimed: the framework’s projected figures came from published studies, never from AskSirion itself.

    What I’d do differently

    Instrument it from day one: how often each band fires, how often people switch readings, and which fields cause the most switches. That would have turned the thresholds from a careful judgement into a tuned one. And revisit prevention: it was cut because interpreting a question took around ten seconds. Most questions now come back in under five, which makes lighter help while typing worth another look.
